title: Going deep, reaching further: What can Boltzmann machines efficiently represent?
authors: Tobias Reinhart, Gemma De les Coves
abstract: While universal approximation theorems theoretically underpin the representation capabilities of machine learning models, they have two shortcomings: They do not focus on efficient representations and they tend to be insensitive to depth and other heuristically important properties. In this work we show that these two shortcomings are intertwined. We prove that machine learning models which are deeper or have higher-order interactions can efficiently represent a larger set of functions, i.e. have larger efficient reach. It follows that deep Boltzmann machines (DBMs) have maximal efficient reach, restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) sub-maximal, and k-body generalizations of RBMs form a hierarchy between the two, even though all are universal. More generally, (i) we provide a full characterization of machine learning models with maximal efficient reach; (ii) we derive separations between deep and shallow models for three representation tasks; and (iii) we prove that the efficient reach of shallow models constitutes an infinite hierarchy indexed by the interaction order. The proofs draw on different methodologies, namely on (i) a recent characterization of universal spin models; (ii) computational complexity bounds for spin models; and (iii) communication complexity bounds applied to shallow models. This work shows that universal machine learning models can strongly differ in their efficient representation capabilities, and provides a theoretical foundation for heuristic observations.
summary: This paper rigorously analyzes the representational power of neural network models by defining 'efficient reach.' It proves that model depth and higher-order interactions are crucial, showing that deep architectures (DBMs) achieve a maximal capacity that shallow models (RBMs) cannot match. This provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the limitations and strengths of different ML architectures in encoding complex physical data.
main_problem: To investigate the 'efficient representation capabilities' (efficient reach) of machine learning models, addressing shortcomings of Universal Approximation Theorems which ignore efficiency and depth.
main_result: Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) are proven to have maximal efficient reach, while shallower models like RBMs have sub-maximal reach, establishing a clear hierarchy based on model depth and interaction order.
method: The work uses theoretical proofs, computational complexity bounds, and communication complexity bounds applied to spin models to characterize the limits of efficient representation.
model_or_system: The models studied are machine learning models, specifically Boltzmann Machines (RBMs, DBMs) framed as spin systems defined by local energy functions (Hamiltonians) on hyperedges.
key_observables: Efficient Reach, KL divergence, Energy Error (RS), and the ability to simulate/approximate specific complex functions (e.g., NP-hard functions).
important_parameters: Model depth (number of layers), interaction order ($k$), and the size of the system ($n$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the formalization of 'visible closure' for ML models, which is shown to be equivalent to maximal efficient reach.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates that DBMs achieve maximal reach, while shallower models form a hierarchy. Table 1 summarizes separations for three tasks comparing shallow vs. maximal models.
paper_structure: The paper first critiques UATs, then provides a full characterization of models with maximal reach using visible closure. It then establishes separations between shallow and deep models for simulating and approximating complex functions, concluding with a hierarchy proof based on interaction order.
why_interesting: The theoretical understanding of which model architectures (deep vs. shallow) can efficiently encode complex physical correlations (like those found in spin glasses or correlated materials) provides a rigorous framework for designing better machine learning models for physics.

Height depicts ordinal inclusion, so that larger efficient reach means the respective models can efficiently represent more targets. We prove that, for depth ≥3, there are models whose efficient reach is max- imal, irrespective of the interaction order. Figure 2: Characterization of maximal models. Set diagram showing properties of machine learning models and their interplay in our characterization of maximal models. Inclusions are not necessarily strict. The three properties given by universal, visible closed and maximal, are such that any two of them imply the third. The area where the three properties hold is depicted in a blue-gray shade. Maximal models are necessarily deep. DBMs are maximal. RBMs and 3-body RBMs are universal, but are not deep, and thus not maximal. We expect most “natural” deep models to be visible closed, and hence most deep universal models to be maximal.

Figure 3: Separation hierarchy for shallow models. Set diagram showing the efficient reach of var- ious machine learning model classes. Each rounded rectangle depicts the maximal set of target functions that the respective model class can efficiently simulate. All shown inclusions are proven to be strict. By definition maximal models have maximal efficient reach, i.e. can efficiently simulate all targets that can be efficiently simulated, including NP-hard functions such as the Ising ground-state function Gn.
